extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (patent prosecutors / applicants / PTAB appeal practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and defending U.S. patent claims to survive §101 rejections (Alice/USPTO Revised Guidance) and related PTAB appeal practice, focusing on showing that claimed subject matter is not a judicial exception or is integrated into a practical application and on Step 2B inventive-concept issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include 'specific features' in claims to show practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide 'specific features' in your patent claims that transform the claims from an ineligible abstract mental process (e.g., 'collecting data, analyzing the data, and displaying results') into an eligible 'practical application' under Alice Step 2A Prong 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and recite claim limitations that do more than state the abstract idea; e.g., the PTAB found that 'downloading the pump configuration files and using them to deliver insulin' were specific features that were not 'insignificant post-solution activity' but an improvement to the operation of an insulin pump. Treat each 'specific feature' individually or in combination as supporting eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support each claimed 'specific feature' in the Specification as an 'improvement to a technology'
rubrics_metrics.description: Include support in the specification that each recited 'specific feature' is an improvement to technology, which the PTAB used to reverse §101 rejections (i.e., treat features as 'an improvement to the operation' of a device or system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the specification to explain how claimed features improve conventional, routine, or traditional systems/methods (examples: improved insulin pump operation; higher performance in speech recognition). Ensure the specification links claimed limitations to concrete technological advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recite technological limitations in claims that integrate the abstract idea into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should themselves contain the technological limitation(s) that integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (do not rely on importing unclaimed specification details).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an improvement is described in the spec (e.g., 'causing a computer program to enter data into a form'), include that limitation in at least some claims (as Campbell shows: claims with the 'enter data into a form' limitation were eligible while broader claims without it were not). Limitations not present in the claims may not be used to avoid an abstract-idea finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include multiple independent and dependent claims as prosecution/appeal backups
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft a variety of claims (broad and narrower) so that if broader claims fail under §101, narrower claims might survive (and vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is a good idea to include multiple independent claims and dependent claims in the appeal as backups in case the PTAB is not persuaded by the broader claim set but is okay with the narrower one.

rubrics_metrics.name: When claims recite mathematical concepts, show how they are integrated into a device or improve it
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting claims involving mathematical concepts or equations, ensure the claims make clear how those concepts are integrated into a device or other practical application and used to improve that device or otherwise solve a problem in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mere mathematical recitation; explain in the specification and claim language how the math is a consequence of device arrangement or used to improve system performance (e.g., Fautz: math used with coil arrangement to improve MR imaging).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bare recitations of mathematical concepts without tying them to systems/implementations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not claim mathematical concepts in the abstract; tie them to specific systems, components, or practical computing steps to avoid being treated as a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely recite calculations or math at a high level (without showing application to a device/system) are at risk of being 'directed to' an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame inventions as improving the functioning of a computer (or other device) when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, describe and claim the invention as an improvement to how a computer or device functions, rather than merely as implementing an abstract concept on a generic computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame improvements generally (improving the functioning of a computer) or tie to specific components or operations. Also, capture specific embodiments of those improvements in the claims so some claims are more likely to survive review (Hsu, Kim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Force Examiners to identify specific alleged ineligible concepts under Step 2A
rubrics_metrics.description: During prosecution, require Examiners to specify the particular judicial exception(s) they allege under prong 1 and prong 2 of Step 2A to clarify rejections and aid in response or appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request that the Examiner identify the specific ineligible concept(s) present in the claims; clarifying the precise alleged exception can help resolve rejections or narrow issues for appeal (Hannun practice tip).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Berkheimer to challenge unsupported Step 2B rejections (require factual support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on Berkheimer v. HP: where an Examiner asserts 'no additional elements' or that claim elements are conventional, require factual support rather than conclusory statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Examiner's Step 2B position lacks evidentiary support that claimed elements are well-understood, routine, conventional, push back and argue the need for factual basis. PTAB has reversed some unsupported Step 2B findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue that claims do not fit into any of the three groupings of abstract ideas when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: It can be worthwhile to make a brief argument that the claims do not fall into the 'three groupings' of abstract ideas identified in the Guidance (mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, and mental processes), as the PTAB may accept this and avoid deeper inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make concise arguments distinguishing the claims from the groupings; this strategy helped in Ex Parte Eronen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import specification limitations into claims; claims control
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations disclosed only in the specification but not recited in the claims cannot be imported into the claims to avoid a §101 rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a specific technical solution is in the specification but not claimed, you cannot rely on it for claim eligibility—capture such solutions in claim language (Hsu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components (processor, memory) are insufficient to make claims patent-eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting a generic 'processor' or 'memory' performing claimed steps does not typically integrate an abstract idea into a practical application; such generic recitations may be treated as mere implementation on a general-purpose computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely use standard computer components to perform abstract ideas are vulnerable; instead, recite how the components are specially configured or how the arrangement provides a technical improvement (Kavis, Kim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims should not be described at a high level of generality when asserting an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: If computer-related limitations are described only at a high level of generality and are well-understood, routine, or conventional, they will likely fail to provide an inventive concept under Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific, concrete claim language and supporting specification showing how elements differ from routine practice; avoid generic, high-level functional language (Kavis Step 2B guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure proper prior-art comparison in obviousness (Section 103) rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: For 103 rejections, the Examiner must properly compare the prior art to the specific recited language of the claims; failure to do so can lead to reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When responding to 103 rejections, point out where the Examiner's comparison is deficient or fails to account for specific claim limitations (Hsu example where 103 rejections were reversed).

rubrics_metrics.name: When mathematical calculations arise from device arrangement and improve system performance, emphasize that connection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed mathematical calculations are a consequence of a device's physical arrangement and used to improve the system (e.g., coil arrangement in MR imaging), emphasize that the claims solve a technical problem and are not mere abstract math.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and claim how the math is applied by the device and how that application improves operation; this supported eligibility in Ex Parte Fautz (citing Thales Visionix).

rubrics_metrics.name: Device/apparatus claims may be more likely to be eligible than corresponding method claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparatus claims that recite a device 'configured to' perform claimed steps and are shown to be 'special-purpose improved machines' may survive §101 where broadly phrased method claims fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both method and device claims; show in the specification and claim language that device claims improve machine operation (Kim: device claims were eligible while method claims were not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming steps that can be performed mentally or with pen and paper
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites steps that can practically be performed in the human mind or with pen and paper (e.g., simple selection or comparison steps), those steps may support a finding of a mental process abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to include computerized, non-mental limitations or special hardware/processing steps that make performance by a person impractical; otherwise the claim may be directed to a mental process (Kim, Kavis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture specific algorithmic/solution details in dependent claims when they provide the improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If particular algorithmic choices or metrics (e.g., Jaccard Distance, Kullback-Leibler divergence) are the basis for an improvement, include those specifics in at least some claims so those claims may be treated as practical applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hsu showed that only claims reciting the specific solutions (the particular disambiguation methods) were found to be practical applications—so include dependent claims that recite the concrete solution details.
